the incidence of major depression in stroke patients was high (22% at 3 months, 13% at 6 months, 11% at 9 months, and 9% at 12 months) and that the prevalence of major depression at 1 year was 9% (95% confidence interval 6% to 12%).
The study was conducted to determine the effectiveness of an educational intervention on the knowledge of stroke patients regarding stroke risk factors and stroke prevention.

the prevalence of major depression in patients with acute ischemic stroke was 15.6% at 1 week, 10.6% at discharge, 7.4% after 6 weeks, and 7.1% at 1 year after stroke onset, and that the risk of developing major depression in patients who did not have depression at baseline was 6.7% at 1-year follow-up.

the relationship between stroke and major depression.
the study of major depressive disorders in a group of stroke patients.
the development and testing of a new model of depression in stroke patients, and the application of this model to the development of a treatment program.

major depression is a common complication after stroke, with an incidence rate ranging from 20% to 30%.
depression after stroke is a complex phenomenon that is influenced by multiple factors and that is associated with poor outcome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found a high frequency of major depression in stroke patients and that the frequency of major depression is not influenced by the severity or location of the stroke.
we found no evidence for an association between stroke and the risk of developing depression.
the prevalence of depression in stroke patients is high, that it is associated with increased mortality, and that its presence is associated with an increased risk of stroke recurrence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is more plastic than we thought and that it is able to compensate for damage.
we have shown the potential of a simple, low-cost, noninvasive method to measure brain activity in stroke patients.
